title: Pulmonary Embolism: The Silent Architect of Hemodynamic Collapse
summary: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) represents a critical medical emergency involving the occlusion of the pulmonary arterial system, typically by a thrombus originating from the deep venous system. Rapid recognition and risk-stratification are the cornerstones of preventing fatal outcomes.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: PE is a mechanical obstruction of the pulmonary vasculature. Epidemiology: Incidence is approx. 60–120 per 100,000 population. It is the third most common cause of cardiovascular death after myocardial infarction and stroke. Mortality rate of untreated PE is up to 30%.

sections.title: Investigations: The Gold Standard
content: Step 1: D-dimer assay (High negative predictive value if low probability).
Step 2: CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) — Test of choice.
Step 3: V/Q Scan (If renal failure or contrast allergy exists).
Step 5: Venous Compression Ultrasound (If DVT suspected).

content.explanation: C: Chest pain, H: Hemoptysis, E: ECG changes (S1Q3T3), S: SOB (Dyspnea), T: Tachycardia.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: 1. Stabilize: Supplemental O2, IV fluids, vasopressors (Norepinephrine).
2. Anticoagulation: LMWH (Enoxaparin 1mg/kg) or UFH (if renal failure).
3. Thrombolysis: rTPA (Alteplase) in massive PE (hemodynamic instability).
4. Embolectomy: Surgical or catheter-directed for absolute contraindications to lysis.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The S1Q3T3 sign on ECG is classic but only present in ~20% of patients.
D-dimer increases with age; use age-adjusted cut-offs (Age x 10 for >50 yrs).
RV dilation (McConnell's sign) on Echo is a hallmark of severe PE.
Early mobilization reduces the risk of post-thrombotic syndrome.
